title: The Southward Offensive
subtitle: The German operational turn south and Soviet defences around Kiev
author: R.G. Cruise
phase: III — The Battle for Strategic Objectives
summary: The German crossing at Novgorod-Seversky threatened the communications behind the Soviet armies defending Ukraine. Soviet headquarters redirected formations through a transport and command system already under severe pressure.
body:
A crossing changes the problem

On 26 August 1941, German troops gained a usable bridge across the Desna at Novgorod-Seversky. The crossing gave the 3rd Panzer Division access to the river’s eastern side and brought the German offensive into a particularly dangerous relationship with the Soviet armies defending Ukraine. Those armies still faced principally westward across the Dnieper. An enemy advancing south behind that defence could threaten the roads and railways that connected it with the Soviet interior. The bridge’s importance lay in the forces and supply columns it could carry towards the communications behind the Soviet defence, well beyond the immediately occupied ground. A river intended to obstruct the Germans had become a route through which they could enlarge their attack. Soviet reporting the following morning acknowledged the loss of Novgorod-Seversky during the afternoon of 26 August and the continuation of the advance southward. Three days after the crossing, a Bryansk Front order explicitly identified the breach on the left of its 13th Army. [1] This was the first operational consequence of the strategic turn examined in [The Decision to Turn South](/articles/barbarossa-the-decision-to-turn-south-1941-08-21) and the divided front described in [A Front Divided](/articles/barbarossa-a-front-divided-1941-08-25). The decision did not bring a fresh German army into Ukraine. It redirected formations already fighting, while other formations had to take over their positions and keep their communications open. Heinz Guderian’s 2nd Panzer Group and Maximilian von Weichs’s 2nd Army moved from Army Group Centre’s southern wing toward the Soviet Southwestern Front. Farther south, Gerd von Rundstedt’s Army Group South was still contesting the Dnieper. Their eventual cooperation would depend on several separate operations succeeding in a useful sequence. On 26 August there was neither a completed encirclement of Kiev nor a simultaneous advance by two equally prepared pincers. [2] The starting problem was the survival of substantial Soviet forces after two months of retreat. David Stahel’s study of Kiev emphasises that the German victory later associated with this campaign emerged from an army already experiencing serious attrition. Army Group South had failed to dispose of the Southwestern Front through its own opening operations, while its motorised formations had accumulated losses and mechanical wear. Assistance from the north offered a way around resistance that frontal pressure had not removed. This interpretation gives the campaign a more demanding explanation than the familiar image of an effortless armoured sweep: German operational opportunity and German material weakness developed together. The southward offensive attempted to exploit the former before the latter made another major undertaking impossible. [3] For Soviet commanders, the threat was more complicated than an approaching column. The Germans were moving near the junction between two fronts, the large Soviet commands responsible for several armies. Holding a river line depended on neighbouring formations remaining in contact, reporting promptly and sharing a workable understanding of the enemy’s direction. The fighting now tested all three conditions. It also exposed a difficult choice: divisions moved north to protect the flank would be unavailable along the Dnieper, where the Germans were preparing crossings of their own. The Soviet response was therefore an attempt to preserve an entire connected defensive system while its northern attachment was coming under attack. [4]

The offensive’s unequal moving parts

Guderian’s account places the opening movement on 25 August. XXIV Motorised Corps sent the 3rd Panzer Division toward Novgorod-Seversky, with the 10th Motorised Division moving through Kholmy and Avdeyevka. The 4th Panzer Division first had to finish fighting near the Sudost before following. XLVII Motorised Corps protected the eastern flank. By the evening of 26 August, the 3rd Panzer Division was at the Desna crossing, whereas the 4th remained engaged southeast of Starodub and the 17th Panzer Division fought near Semtsy, south of Pochep. These dispositions describe an offensive assembling through combat, rather than a compact formation already moving at a single speed. [5] The distinction between a panzer group and its leading tanks matters here. A panzer group was a command containing several formations, including motorised infantry and supporting units. Its capacity to penetrate depended on the concentration of armour, infantry, artillery and engineers at a particular point. Its capacity to exploit that penetration depended on maintaining connections behind and beside them. The American Army’s operational history describes Guderian leaving substantial strength to contain Bryansk Front while he advanced south. This was an immediate deduction from the force available for the main objective. Soviet resistance on a flank could slow the offensive without physically stopping the leading division at its next road junction. [2] Infantry armies performed a related but different task. Weichs’s 2nd Army approached the northern side of the Ukrainian theatre after the fighting around Gomel. Its progress brought pressure against Soviet formations that might otherwise have turned against Guderian’s western flank. Yet infantry could not simply reproduce the movement of selected motorised detachments. It had its own defended routes to open, artillery to bring forward and marching columns to supply. A successful armoured advance could thus increase the distance between the spearhead and the infantry expected to make its gains secure. The operational relationship was reciprocal: the tanks created a threat deep in the Soviet rear, while the infantry helped prevent that threat from becoming an isolated excursion. [2] There was a further complication in the organisation of Soviet command. A Bryansk Front order issued at 18.00 on 25 August transferred the forces of the Central Front to Bryansk Front from midnight at the beginning of 26 August. It then prescribed a new army composition, with some arrangements taking effect on 28 August. Andrei Yeremenko’s headquarters was consequently absorbing formations and establishing control while the Germans were attacking the same geographical seam. This was more than the replacement of one name on a map. Existing reports, supply relationships and subordinate headquarters had to be fitted into a new command structure during a moving battle. [1] The evening report for 26 August shows how unevenly that process worked. Communications with 50th Army functioned by telephone, telegraph and liaison officers; the telegraph and radio connections with 13th Army were intermittent. An operational group was being established around Khutor-Mikhailovsky to control forces inherited from Central Front. These details help explain why a headquarters could possess a strategic appreciation of danger without possessing an accurate, timely picture of every threatened crossing. Recognising the danger was only the beginning of a response. A report had to reach headquarters, produce an order suited to the forces available, and return through the damaged communications network before the threatened formation’s position changed again. [1]

Rivers, roads and the new Soviet flank

The Desna, Seym and Dnieper formed connected obstacles rather than three interchangeable blue lines. The Desna approached the Dnieper from the northeast, while the Seym fed into the Desna farther upstream. A German advance from the Starodub region toward the rear of the Southwestern Front therefore encountered successive river valleys and a limited set of useful crossings. Securing one passage did not provide an uninterrupted road to Kiev’s eastern communications. It changed the next military problem: Soviet forces could contest the bridgehead, threaten its approaches or hold another river farther south. The Southwestern Front’s orders consequently identified routes toward Krolevets, Vorozhba and Konotop, as well as stretches of riverbank. The command was trying to protect a network through which the enemy could penetrate. [4] The creation of the 40th Army gave this concern an institutional form. Assigned to the Southwestern Front on 26 August under Kuzma Podlas, the army was placed on its endangered northern side. The detailed directive issued two days later listed the 293rd and 135th Rifle Divisions, the 10th Tank Division, the 2nd Airborne Corps and the 5th Antitank Artillery Brigade among its formations. Its headquarters was to be at Konotop. The task was to prevent a breakthrough toward the routes just identified and protect the front against attack from the north. These were concrete defensive responsibilities, even though the order’s list of formations cannot by itself establish their actual strength, equipment or readiness at every moment. [4] The presence of airborne troops is instructive. In this setting an airborne corps designation did not imply that the formation was about to conduct a parachute operation. The directive required elements of the 2nd Airborne Corps to be brought by motor transport to the Korop–Maloye Ustye sector. It also ordered the 3rd Airborne Corps to concentrate by road in the Konotop area by the morning of 31 August. Their usefulness rested on the availability of organised infantry that could be shifted toward a threatened point. Their mobility rested on trucks, suitable roads and time. An airborne title did not exempt soldiers from the transport constraints affecting the rest of the army. [4] The same directive required the 5th Army to continue holding the Dnieper while protecting itself against attack from the north. At least one division was to defend a specified stretch of the Desna by the end of 29 August; at least two divisions were to be retained near the junction with 40th Army. The 37th Army had to hold Kiev, with its flanks tied to the Dnieper and its centre occupying the fortified approaches west of the city. The 26th and 38th Armies continued the defence farther south. Each instruction was intelligible in isolation. Together they reveal the strain of trying to preserve a long river front while constructing a second front at an angle to it. [4] Nor was every formation immediately available for the task assigned to it. The document placed the 304th Rifle Division in reserve while it completed its armament and left the 81st Rifle Division reorganizing around Lubny. Such details correct the impression created by orderly symbols on a situation map. A division could exist in an order of battle while still requiring weapons, replacement personnel or reorganisation before effective employment. The northern defence was therefore a race between the German advance and the Soviet ability to turn administrative assignments into coordinated fighting power. That race remained open at the end of August; its outcome should not be read backward from the catastrophe of September. [4]

Resistance that consumed the advance

The Bryansk Front reports show local resistance continuing beside the German breakthrough. At Semtsy, south of Pochep, the Germans attacked after repeated air bombardment and took the settlement during the afternoon of 26 August. The following morning’s Soviet report stated that a counterattack had recovered it at 22.00. These are headquarters reports, not a complete reconstruction of the engagement, but their sequence is revealing. On the same day that the Germans gained a major crossing farther south, a nearby sector was changing hands through attack and counterattack. The front was not dissolving uniformly. Its unevenness forced German commanders to decide where to press ahead and where to employ troops that might otherwise have joined the main thrust. [1] By 29 August, Yeremenko had ordered a mobile group under Arkady Yermakov to attack toward the threatened sector. The grouping combined the 108th Tank Division, 141st Tank Brigade and 4th Cavalry Division. The order prescribed separate routes, Sudost crossings and successive objectives, with the intended arrival around Novgorod-Seversky by the end of 31 August. The cavalry was to follow behind the tank formations and cooperate in destroying the opposing forces. This was an effort to strike the side of the penetration and restore the connection between Soviet armies. Its existence establishes a deliberate response; the ambitious deadlines establish the command’s expectations, not proof that the objectives were reached. [1] The arrangements for cooperation are as revealing as the movement arrows. The air command was instructed to cover the mobile group’s march and crossings, support its attacks, and send an operational officer and a U-2 aircraft to each of the principal armoured formations. A radio centre was to be established around Trubchevsk. These provisions addressed practical weaknesses that earlier fighting had exposed: formations needed to find one another, communicate their positions and connect air attacks with ground movement. The order does not demonstrate that these arrangements worked smoothly. It does demonstrate that Soviet command was attempting to solve a coordination problem, rather than merely supplying another mass of troops to an undifferentiated counterattack. [1]

A minefield on the wrong side of the report

The Bryansk Front’s report for 26 August recorded a small incident involving the 108th Tank Division. Three T-40 light tanks conducting reconnaissance near Sloboda entered a minefield laid by Soviet troops. A lieutenant was killed, a Red Army soldier wounded and two tanks put out of action. The report gives no names and does not establish who failed to pass on the minefield’s location. It nevertheless preserves a human and mechanical cost that disappears in a map showing only German and Soviet positions. Defensive preparations could become a danger to friendly movement when information failed to travel with them. The division was in front reserve, preparing for employment against the German penetration; its losses here occurred before such a contest could be reduced to a comparison of opposing tank strengths. This is a documented accident, not evidence that all Soviet minefields or reconnaissance procedures were equally defective. [1]

Moving supplies and making roads

Bryansk Front’s rear-services directive of 25 August provides an unusually clear view of what sustaining the response required. Its armies were assigned railway sections leading through Bryansk and the approaches from Orel and Dmitriyev-Lgovsky. Ammunition stocks were to be built at several levels: with the troops, at army depots and at front bases. Food and fodder reserves were likewise distributed, with fifteen days prescribed at front bases and smaller reserves farther forward. These were targets for an operating supply system. They must not be mistaken for evidence that every specified stock already existed. The order shows what headquarters wanted available as it prepared to defend, regroup and counterattack. [1] Every army was also to have at least two prepared roads suitable for motor and horse transport. Roads and bridges were to remain passable in different weather conditions, and local road authorities and the civilian population were to be used extensively to bring them into condition. Difficult stretches required traffic regulation and tractors ready to assist vehicles. The plan was due on the evening of 26 August, with the road preparations to be completed by 1 September. These deadlines placed repair work inside the battle’s timetable. A formation moving toward the Desna could be delayed by a damaged bridge or an obstructed approach even when its headquarters had fuel somewhere in the rear. [1] The civilian population thus entered the operational record as labour required to keep the army moving. The directive does not tell us how particular villages supplied workers, how voluntary participation was distinguished from compulsion, or what happened to families when the front moved again. It does establish that civilian work formed part of the command’s practical solution. Roads used for military supply also carried evacuation traffic and connected farms to markets and households to neighbouring settlements. The demand for military movement imposed priorities on that shared infrastructure. Civilians experienced the offensive not only through bombardment and occupation but through the appropriation of time, transport and physical labour needed to maintain an army’s resistance. [1] Medical evacuation ran in the opposite direction. The directive provided for wounded and sick personnel to move by hospital trains from Bryansk and Dmitriyev-Lgovsky toward the evacuation system around Orel, Livny, Yelets and Mtsensk. It also required army medical facilities to be organised near the principal rail connections. This was a planned chain of movement from fighting units to transport and onward treatment. Its dependence on rail access explains another consequence of the German penetration: a threatened communications route endangered both the arrival of ammunition and the removal of casualties. Holding a junction could preserve the possibility of care as well as the capacity to continue fighting. [1] German mobility depended on a similarly layered system, although one increasingly stretched away from its original bases. Fuel delivered to the theatre still had to reach the divisions; replacement parts still had to reach repair personnel; damaged vehicles still had to be recovered. The German Army’s early September assessment, summarized in its postwar American study, reported exhausted fuel stockpiles and shortages that sometimes interrupted operations in the south. Its 4 September tank assessment distinguished vehicles available for employment from those under repair and those disabled. Those later figures cannot describe every division on 26 August, but they confirm that the turn south was being executed during an accumulating maintenance problem, before autumn weather could provide an all-purpose explanation for German difficulties. [6]

Grossman’s road out of the retreat

Vasily Grossman’s notebooks from the retreat through Belarus and northeastern Ukraine preserve people whom operational reports usually leave unnamed. In the edited diary selection, an older woman waits beside a passing column in the hope of seeing her son. Others offer soldiers milk, cucumbers, apples and curds. Grossman also notices households being abandoned and refugees sharing roads with livestock, guns and military vehicles. These observations belong to the August–September journey; the published extract does not justify assigning each scene to 26 August. Their value lies in showing civilian action amid disruption. The people beside the road were searching, feeding, deciding what to carry and trying to maintain contact with relatives. Grossman was an involved Soviet correspondent, not a detached surveyor of public opinion, and his impressions cannot speak for every village. They nevertheless restore individual purposes to a landscape that military records chiefly describe as routes and obstacles. [7]

The southern front and the wider war

Farther south, Kleist’s 1st Panzer Group was still involved in the struggle for the Dnieper approaches. Southern Front’s report covering 15–31 August described combat around Dnepropetrovsk, Zaporozhye, Berislav and Kherson, alongside the regrouping and replenishment of Soviet formations. Its account dated the evacuation of Dnepropetrovsk to the early hours of 25 August, after sustained fighting on the approaches. These operations had their own objectives: crossings toward the industrial districts farther east, and approaches toward the Crimea in the lower river sector. They were not yet the northward movement from Kremenchuk that would later form the southern arm of the Kiev encirclement. [8] The lower river remained actively contested. A Soviet attempt to regain Kherson on 24 August failed; the same summary described renewed German pressure at Berislav on 26 August and the Soviet withdrawal across the river during the following night. On 30 August German troops established a foothold around Kakhovka after artillery and air preparation. These developments show why it is misleading to imagine Army Group South waiting in readiness for Guderian. Its formations were fighting their way through a broad river system against opponents still capable of resistance and counterattack. The later concentration for the decisive encirclement would require selection among these competing tasks. [8] Western policy operated on another timescale. In the Roosevelt–Churchill message transmitted officially to Moscow on 18 August, the two leaders proposed a conference to determine longer-term Soviet requirements and the allocation of shared resources. They promised continuing shipments while acknowledging that British and American resources, although large, had competing demands. This correspondence matters because it records a developing commitment to Soviet survival without implying that promised equipment was already available to Podlas or Yeremenko. A shipment leaving a Western port and a weapon reaching a threatened division were separate events, connected by voyages, unloading, assembly and onward transport. The immediate defence of the Desna still depended on the forces and material that Soviet commanders could bring into the battle at hand. [9]

Children beyond the operational map

The danger created by German occupation was already visible behind Army Group South. In her study of military chaplains, Doris Bergen examines the August murder of Jewish children at Bila Tserkva and the later accounts of German clergymen who had attempted an intervention. She also restores testimony from Jews whose experiences complicate a story centred entirely on those Germans. Isaac Piatsetski, a Polish Jewish refugee interviewed in 1998, remembered seeing a train evacuating children before the occupation. Bergen treats his belief about its eventual destination more cautiously than his recollection of the departure itself. The distinction matters: an evacuation could be a real act of rescue without every subsequent stage being recoverable from one witness. The contrast between children transported away and children trapped under German authority establishes what was at stake when military routes remained open. It also connects the displacement begun in Poland in 1939 with the new emergency in Soviet Ukraine. [10]

The position reached

By the end of 26 August, the Germans had gained a significant crossing and Soviet headquarters faced an urgent threat to the northern connection of the Ukrainian defence. They had not yet converted that opportunity into a closed pocket. The Soviet orders of the following days show additional formations being assigned, river sectors being reinforced and a counterstroke being organised against the penetration. They also expose the limits of that response: incomplete concentrations, formations still reorganizing, interrupted communications and a transport system required to support several urgent purposes at once. The Germans benefited from those weaknesses while encountering enough resistance to consume strength along their expanding flanks. [1][4] The offensive’s importance lay in the relationship between these processes. A successful crossing threatened the Soviet rear; that threat compelled new deployments; new deployments competed with the defence of the Dnieper and with the transport needed to sustain it. German commanders sought to make those pressures develop faster than Soviet headquarters could resolve them. This remained a contest over time and usable connections as much as distance. While it unfolded in Ukraine, the war’s northern theatre was reaching a different crisis of withdrawal and transport. At Tallinn, troops and civilians were preparing to escape through a sea route whose apparent openness concealed dangers as consequential as any river crossing. [The Baltic Withdrawal](/articles/barbarossa-the-baltic-withdrawal-1941-08-29) follows that operation and the people whose survival depended upon it.

sourceMethod: Numbered citations lead to the sources below; each entry lists the passages cited and links back to its first use. Contemporary orders establish intentions, while reports contain the information, estimates and gaps known to their authors. Retrospective military accounts and testimony are identified and assessed alongside documentary evidence and scholarship. English paraphrases of Russian, Ukrainian and German texts are by the atlas unless a published translator is named. Archival references reproduced in published sources do not imply direct archival inspection. Events after the chapter date are dated explicitly. The companion map is a dated regional military reconstruction; its feature sources and precision notes distinguish reported positions from approximate connecting edges.
